AI INVESTMENT ATMOSPHERE · PUBLIC EQUITY RESEARCH

AI investment is expanding.
Growth is slowing. Can profits catch up?

Four equally weighted pillars track adoption, monetization, hyperscalers and infrastructure. The research follows that activity into capacity, monetization, cash generation and returns, then tests it against equity and credit markets.

Core score: June 2026 S1 · Equity and CDS observations through 2026-11-24 S4S5 · Financial periods vary by company; supplementary score adjustments retain their 16 Sep vintage.
CORE62.5ABOVE HISTORICAL NORM
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY · INVESTMENT CONCLUSION

AI investment expands as growth slows and the earnings test becomes more demanding.

Analyst review · 17 November 2026 · changes versus the prior saved November 10 data snapshot

AI investment continues to expand, but growth is becoming less uniform and the earnings test more demanding. The November 17 refresh adds business-adoption and spending observations, updates investment estimates and extends market coverage. Broader adoption and stronger GPU rental pricing coexist with slower usage and spending momentum.

The five covered hyperscalers’ next-four-fiscal-quarter CapEx estimate rose 0.8% to $1.10T versus the prior saved update. The larger signal is the trajectory: quarterly headline spending rises from $230B in Q3 2026 to an estimated $309B in Q3 2027, while year-over-year growth slows from 118% to 34%. A larger investment base supports suppliers, while slower growth raises the risk of earnings expectations outrunning demand.

October Ramp paid adoption reached 56.8%. In the separate matched-model sample, lower effective unit costs offset higher volume and spending fell 2.0% in the window ending October 25. OpenRouter estimated spending grew 22.1%, with historical values repriced in this refresh. Subsequent token-volume and consumer-spending growth moderated. A broad acceleration in paid demand remains to be demonstrated.

The pillar review adds a profitability concern from the previously collected Anthropic filing. Q3 compute expense grew faster than revenue, and adjusted operating margin fell from 19% to 15%. The reported loss also reflects a material non-cash charitable charge. Commercial scale is increasing alongside pressure on the share of revenue retained as profit.

Infrastructure is progressing at different speeds. September order growth slowed while import growth accelerated, and completed-quarter operational capacity additions eased in Q3. GPU rentals strengthened, but memory prices diverged. These observations warrant attention to product mix, delivery lags and power constraints. The partial Q4 capacity observation provides limited evidence about the full-quarter pace.

Market confirmation remains mixed. Semiconductor relative performance recovered but remained negative, while BBB credit pressure eased modestly over the latest week. The latest weekly activity pulse is 55.2 with six of eight inputs; its missing spending signals limit the evidence of a broad upturn. Cash-funding and ROIC coverage still largely ends in June, leaving the latest investment increase ahead of comparable return evidence.

Investment conclusionConfirmation requires sustained paid-spending growth, stronger cloud profit and operating cash flow catching up with investment. Further cost pressure, repeated CapEx estimate cuts or renewed credit widening would weaken the outlook. Improving cash coverage and incremental ROIC would strengthen it.

Chart events and sources
  1. 18 Mar 2024 · Blackwell announced — NVIDIA announced its Blackwell computing platform, a milestone in accelerator supply.
  2. 20–21 Jan 2025 · R1 / Stargate — DeepSeek released R1 on 20 January; OpenAI announced Stargate on 21 January. Model affordability and infrastructure commitments provide context for adoption and investment. Stargate announcement.
  3. 24 Feb 2025 · Claude Code preview — Anthropic introduced Claude Code in a limited research preview. Agentic coding adds repeated model calls for code inspection, editing, tool use and testing.
  4. 2 Apr 2025 · Reciprocal tariffs — U.S. reciprocal tariffs were announced, relevant to equipment trade and supply-chain investment.
  5. 16 May 2025 · Codex agent preview — OpenAI launched the cloud software-engineering agent Codex in research preview, allowing delegated tasks to run in separate environments. This marks the agent product launch, not the earlier Codex model.
  6. 29 Jan 2026 · OpenClaw announcement — The project announced the OpenClaw name after starting as Clawd in November 2025. It reported more than 100,000 GitHub stars and 2 million visitors in a week. This is a distribution milestone for general-purpose agents, not its first release or a measure of paid usage.
  7. 11 Nov 2026 · NVIDIA CEO resignation — NVIDIA’s board accepted Jensen Huang’s resignation effective November 11 and named Colette Kress interim CEO. NVIDIA announced the transition on November 12.
  8. 19 Nov 2026 · Anthropic IPO debut (expected) — Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share on November 18 and said ANT was expected to begin trading on Nasdaq on November 19.

Calculation and coverage
PillarScoring signals
AdoptionCurrent and expected business AI use and Ramp paid adoption use rate levels. OpenRouter and Ramp token volumes use separate percentiles of month-over-month growth in the trailing three-month average.
MonetizationBusiness paid demand uses YoY growth in the three-month average of Ramp median spend per employee and 28-day spending growth from Ramp and OpenRouter. Consumer card spending compares the latest four weeks with the prior four. Frontier labs use log annualized revenue levels.

Four equal nominal 25% pillars. Adoption combines breadth and usage. Monetization combines business paid demand, consumer paid demand and annualized lab revenue scale. Missing weights are redistributed within each pillar, then across available pillars. Source dates identify carried-forward observations.

Monthly levels use matched complete four-week windows. Token growth compares the trailing three-month average with the prior month’s three-month average, requiring four consecutive monthly levels. Each growth rate is ranked against its source’s observations through June 2026. Ties receive the midpoint percentile. Ramp is displayed in publisher index/day units. A score of 50 represents the median rank for token-volume growth and the baseline mean for the z-scored signals.

The matched Ramp and OpenRouter spending-growth baselines each contain six observations from January through June 2026. The consumer card baseline covers the same months. Lab calibration uses 12 OpenAI disclosures and 11 Anthropic disclosures. These calibrations are provisional.

Level contribution is effective weight multiplied by the score’s difference from 50. Core attribution sums contributions by pillar. Within a selected pillar, effective weights are expressed as shares of that pillar. Monthly impact is the change in contribution, including weight changes.

Sources, methodology and scope

  1. (1) Data source and reliability

    The core uses saved Bloomberg macro and CapEx inputs, BTOS surveys, Ramp business data, OpenRouter rankings and prices, U.S. consumer card spending, and reported frontier-lab revenue run rates. Coverage and observation dates differ by signal.

    S1S2S9S10S14S18

  2. (2) Methodology

    Methodology v3.5 assigns 25% nominal weight to each of four pillars. Adoption combines rate levels and token-volume growth percentiles. Monetization combines business spending, consumer card spending growth and log annualized lab revenue levels. Hyperscalers scores combined trailing-four-quarter CapEx growth. Infrastructure combines physical activity and hardware pricing. Token scores use separate historical percentiles. Other scores use 50 + 15 × z-score, bounded to 0–100. Available constituents share the pillar’s weight in proportion to their nominal weights, and available pillars share the core weight equally.

  3. (3) Scope and other necessary information

    The chart shades the range of observed constituent scores. Quarterly Hyperscalers scores repeat across their quarter’s months. E identifies estimates from the five-company CapEx scenario. Later core scores use the available observed pillars and are provisional. Carried-forward readings retain their source dates. The fixed calibration through June 2026 makes this a retrospective series.

Scoring and coverage

Each signal compares four completed weeks with the prior four, requiring all eight observations. OpenRouter requires seven covered days per week; Ramp requires at least 95% matched-price coverage. OpenRouter and Ramp use 31 matched weeks in 2025. Card spending uses 45 matched weeks from November 30, 2025 through October 4, 2026. Token affordability measures the change in tokens per dollar implied by the Bloomberg SDLLMTK price proxy. It uses 39 calibration weeks through October 18, 2026. Each price week requires seven saved daily values, which can include carried quotes. Hardware prices use Bloomberg observations from AI_Infra.xlsx. Weekly averages require at least four saved weekdays in a completed week. Rising prices score as stronger pricing momentum. Hardware baselines use qualifying weeks through November 1, 2026. Each score uses 50 + 15 × (growth − baseline mean) / sample standard deviation, bounded to 0–100. This retrospective calibration is not a real-time backtest.

01 · CORE PILLAR · 25% NOMINAL WEIGHT

Adoption

Adoption breadth and token activity track how widely AI is used.

Ramp paid adoption reached 56.8% of sampled businesses in October, up 1.0 percentage point from revised September. Current and expected business-use surveys measure breadth, while OpenRouter and Ramp token activity measure usage in their respective samples.

Analyst review · 2026-11-17

Adoption splits its weight equally between breadth and usage. Breadth uses three adoption-rate levels. OpenRouter and Ramp usage each rank month-over-month growth in their trailing three-month average against their own history through June 2026.

OpenRouter routed traffic and Ramp sampled business activity cover different populations. Their volumes are normalized separately. The latest complete source readings carry forward with their dates, so a held reading is visible when the next monthly observation is unavailable.

What to watch. Watch current use, expected use and observed paid adoption together with sustained token activity. Compare usage breadth with the business paid-demand evidence in Monetization to assess how usage translates into spending.

Sources & methodology

Source: OpenRouter (openrouter.ai/rankings), as of 2026-11-23T02:10:49.451Z. Licensed under CC BY 4.0.

Prompt and completion tokens are counted using each provider’s tokenizer. This is routed usage on OpenRouter; it does not measure users or the entire AI market. Free and dated model variants stay separate. Other includes the source’s aggregated long tail plus every named model outside the selected top 10. Missing daily source buckets appear as gaps; weekly averages require all seven days. Model detail breaks down the existing OpenRouter volume signal without adding another core constituent.

Daily ranges end at the latest saved complete UTC day. Weekly ranges end at the last completed Sunday and use only whole Monday–Sunday weeks, so their dates can differ from OpenRouter’s trailing-seven-day leaderboard. “Not named” means a model was not separately reported in that bucket; any tokens remain in Other. Named-model totals can understate full model usage when a model falls below the source’s daily top 50.

Cost recovery depends on volume and unit margins.

Buyer cost per successful task can fall through model efficiency, higher success rates or lower prices. It does not directly measure revenue per token. More paid volume is needed only if contribution dollars per task fall while the capital-recovery requirement is unchanged.

Capital-recovery assumptions and sensitivity
CAPITAL RECOVERY SENSITIVITY

Daily successful tasks required per $1B of capital

Illustrative mapping of buyer task cost to seller revenue: at fixed capital and contribution margin, a lower assumed price requires more paid tasks. Actual infrastructure billing and serving economics may differ.

Sources, methodology and scope

  1. (1) Data source and reliability

    Workbook prices/run costs, Epoch model coverage and exact model matches to SWE-bench Verified or DeepSWE Pass@1. Benchmark results are system-and-harness observations; unmatched records retain explicit workbook assumptions.

    S13

  2. (2) Methodology

    Estimate cost per successful task from attempt cost and benchmark success. Frontier anchors lie within five ECI points of the dated capability leader, with historical Epoch coverage for legacy models. Best value is the lowest Tier-A observed cost among models with at least 50% success in a trailing 180-day window. Recovery sensitivity assumes a five-year asset life, 10% required return and the displayed margin scenarios: tasks × price × contribution margin ≥ depreciation + required return.

  3. (3) Scope and other necessary information

    This is a derived buyer-side price-performance measure; task expenditure is not infrastructure-owner revenue or profit. Benchmark success is a proxy, not production reliability. Model, harness, reasoning and token assumptions limit comparability. MiniMax, DeepSeek and GLM candidates begin in August 2025 because earlier collected observations lack both comparable success and run cost. The shaded frontier/value gap is not an uncertainty interval.

02 · CORE PILLAR · 25% NOMINAL WEIGHT

Monetization

Business paid demand connects AI usage with spending and revenue scale.

Business paid demand combines Ramp median spending, Ramp matched spending growth and OpenRouter estimated routed-spending growth. Consumer card spending grew 3.7% in the four-week window ending November 8. OpenAI and Anthropic annualized revenue levels track the scale of commercialization.

Analyst review · 2026-11-17

In the matched Ramp window ending October 25, volume rose 30.7%, effective unit cost fell 25.0% and spending declined 2.0%. OpenRouter estimated spending grew 22.1%, down from 28.1% in the preceding window. Effective cost includes model mix and commercial terms. Broader adoption can therefore coexist with slower spending growth.

Anthropic Q3 revenue rose 46.7% sequentially to $16.956B. Compute and infrastructure expense grew 77.5% to $9.863B, increasing from 48.1% to 58.2% of revenue. Its reported operating loss was $567M. Adjusted operating income rose from $2.235B to $2.463B, while adjusted margin fell from 19% to 15%; the reported result includes a $1.960B non-cash charitable charge. Cost growth and other expenses both matter to the earnings assessment.

OpenAI’s collected run rate remains approximately $50B at end-September, reported October 8. Run-rate, recognized-revenue and funding-valuation dates differ. Rising valuations increase the earnings required to support them; prospective IPO values remain uncertain.

What to watch. Watch sustained business spending growth, consumer demand and disclosed revenue scale alongside compute expense, operating margins and cash generation. OpenRouter spending is a routed-demand proxy across mixed use cases; Ramp observes sampled business payments.

Volume and price breakdown

Each change compares four completed weeks with the preceding monthly observation window. A five-week gap between endpoints leaves one week outside both windows. Ramp uses the same matched spending/token pairs within each window; changing model composition can affect growth. Growth = volume change + price change + interaction. For Ramp’s indexed feed, dividing the relative spending and volume changes gives an implied unit-cost change. The two spending-growth signals enter Monetization business paid demand at 5% nominal core weight each, using their provisional January–June 2026 baselines. Their source samples remain separate.

Sources, methodology and scope

  1. (1) Data source and reliability

    Workbook records for OpenAI and Anthropic compiled from media reports and investor disclosures. Run rates are estimates, not audited recognized revenue; reported floors and approximations remain labeled.

    S10

  2. (2) Methodology

    Separate full-company recognized revenue from ARR and annualized run rate; FY2025 recognized revenue appears separately in the cards. Compare growth from end-2025. OpenAI’s September 29, 2026 observation is plotted at approximately $70B, based on Reuters and Axios reporting around DevDay, not a verified official DevDay revenue disclosure. Earlier floors remain floor observations. Excludes product/division records and period-interpolation observations.

  3. (3) Scope and other necessary information

    ARR annualizes a point-in-time pace and is neither recognized revenue nor cash collection. Reporting dates and definitions limit direct ranking. Audited quarterly revenue, margins, cash burn and contracted compute demand are needed to connect lab revenue with infrastructure economics.

03 · HYPERSCALERS

Hyperscalers

Capital spending reaches new highs as growth slows sharply.

The November 17 next-four-fiscal-quarter CapEx estimate rose $8.6B, or 0.8%, to $1.10T versus the prior saved November 10 snapshot. Microsoft accounts for $5.6B of the revision. Reported CapEx is unchanged between those imports.

Analyst review · 2026-11-17

The five-company headline total rises from $230.4B in Q3 2026 to an estimated $309.4B in Q3 2027, while year-over-year growth slows from 117.8% to 34.3%. Quarters group native fiscal period ends, including Oracle’s different calendar. Higher comparison bases contribute to deceleration. Supplier revenue can keep growing while its growth rate and earnings momentum moderate.

Cloud revisions differ by company. Alphabet’s 2027 Q2 cloud-revenue and RPO estimates increased $1.26B and $11.70B between the November 9 and 17 captures. Microsoft’s near-term CapEx estimates rose while commercial RPO estimates eased. RPO conversion timing and segment profit are the next tests; business scopes differ across issuers.

What to watch. Track comparable-quarter estimate revisions, reported cloud operating profit and operating-cash-flow growth relative to cash CapEx. Repeated investment cuts would reinforce the slowdown. Improving cash coverage and incremental ROIC would support a more constructive return assessment.

Sources, methodology and scope

  1. (1) Data source and reliability

    S8 · Indexlist.xlsx — Hyperscaler Core Data Value. Cached Bloomberg quarterly NOPAT, equity, debt, cash and lease fields for all five companies. Core results use equity + debt − cash and short-term investments. Long-term investments are not available in this sheet. Snapshot hash: f60e92129d05…

  2. (2) Methodology

    Profit numerator

    NOPAT is net operating profit after tax. Four consecutive Bloomberg quarterly observations form the trailing-year profit numerator.

    Core invested capital

    Shareholders’ equity + interest-bearing debt − cash and short-term investments. Beginning and ending balances are averaged. Full cash deduction is a simplifying assumption, not an estimate of excess cash.

    Incremental return

    Change in TTM Bloomberg NOPAT divided by change in average invested capital. Eight quarters is the preferred horizon; four quarters remains diagnostic. Results are withheld for non-positive capital changes or increases below 5% of the earlier capital base.

    Lease sensitivity

    Operating and finance lease liabilities are added once when debt treatment is confirmed. The sensitivity is approximate because implied lease interest is not added back to NOPAT.

  3. (3) Scope and other necessary information

    Consolidated ROIC includes mature businesses and non-AI investment. Without attributable AI capital, NOPAT and a cost of capital, it cannot establish AI value creation. Excluded from both atmosphere scores.

    Microsoft: Direct Bloomberg NOPAT and core invested-capital fields available.

04 · PHYSICAL INFRASTRUCTURE

Infrastructure

Capacity expands, while orders, deliveries and pricing move at different speeds.

Completed September communication-equipment and IT-equipment orders grew 25.7% and 13.7% year over year, slowing from 41.6% and 16.5% in August. Telecom and computer import growth accelerated to 75.6% and 177.8%. These nominal series cover different products and delivery stages.

Analyst review · 2026-11-17

Covered modeled operational IT capacity rose from 8.00 GW in Q2 to 9.38 GW in Q3. Quarterly additions slowed from 2.48 GW to 1.38 GW. The 9.80 GW Q4 observation is partial through November 6 and cannot establish a full-quarter slowdown. This facility evidence is retained from the earlier snapshot.

By November 15, four-week B200 and H100 rental-price momentum reached +11.6% and +7.0%. DDR5 rose 5.0%, while NAND fell 7.2%. Firmer GPU pricing alongside slower orders and mixed memory prices suggests uneven product availability. Power, permitting and commissioning delays can also slow the conversion of spending into revenue.

What to watch. Watch completed-quarter capacity additions, order growth, delivery timing and sustained GPU pricing together. Paid utilization and revenue per installed unit would provide stronger evidence of capital productivity. Current capacity estimates leave those outcomes unmeasured.

07 · SUPPLEMENTARY RESEARCH

Policy

U.S. data center permitting and project delays

Permit freezes and zoning denials can push back or prevent delivery of the power and facilities needed for AI compute. The effect depends on the project stage and whether the rule covers existing approvals.

In the Nov. 3, 2026 midterms, voters favored restricting data center development in 40 of 41 local ballot contests tracked by Ballotpedia. The results included advisory measures and votes on individual rezoning proposals. Project schedules depend on how each measure applies. Ballotpedia election results

05 · SUPPLEMENTARY RESEARCH

Funding & recovery

Long-lived commitments raise the cost of a demand or delivery shortfall.

Large compute commitments and supplier financing make the timing of revenue and cash collection increasingly important. The retained transaction records identify dependencies across labs, cloud providers and equipment vendors.

Analyst review · 2026-11-17

Anthropic disclosed $313.8B of fixed or minimum commitments at September 30, with terms of one to 20 years. These future obligations create a recovery hurdle that persists through changes in demand and pricing.

Supplier investment, customer purchases and guarantees can connect funding conditions across the chain. Overlapping arrangements, future commitments and contingent support require separate treatment when assessing exposure. Training-cost scenarios cover only part of the full cost base.

What to watch. Watch cash collections, funding maturities, guarantee triggers and changes to contracted capacity. Delayed deployment combined with fixed payments would increase funding pressure.

Sources, methodology and scope

  1. (1) Data source and reliability

    Epoch AI frontier-model and accelerator datasets. Training costs are compute estimates in constant 2023 USD; disclosure is sparse and the latest model records may lack costs.

    S12

  2. (2) Methodology

    Plot cost-bearing model observations and annual median/interquartile range; shading shows the interquartile range of covered estimates. Compare accelerator release-price performance. Training-cost recovery divides estimated compute cost by the illustrated contribution-margin assumptions, which must already allow for variable serving costs.

  3. (3) Scope and other necessary information

    Training compute is neither total model-development cost nor customer API price. Covered cost observations end on 2025-07-09; model coverage extends to 2026-09-03. Recovery sensitivities exclude serving, research payroll, failed experiments, data, financing and overhead. Hardware comparisons exclude systems, networking, power, utilization and purchasing terms. These sensitivities are not forecasts.

Market

Semiconductor performance recovers as financing pressure remains selective.

The four-week XSOX relative-return measure versus SPXT improved from −20.9% on November 6 to −7.8% on November 13. Relative performance remains negative, leaving market confirmation incomplete.

Analyst review · 2026-11-17

Credit data now extend to November 17. The covered BBB group’s median spread change relative to the IG benchmark eased to +18.5 bp since year-end from +19.6 bp on November 10. Oracle CDS was approximately 181 bp. This is modest recent relief within a still uneven financing environment.

The November 15 weekly pulse is 55.2 with six of eight signals. Ramp matched spending and consumer card spending are missing from that week. The latest complete reading was 46.9 on November 1. Changing coverage limits comparison of headline scores.

What to watch. Look for broadening equity participation, a full-coverage improvement in activity and sustained credit stabilization. Renewed spread widening alongside weaker demand revisions would raise downside risk. Assess bond issuance on matched complete periods.

Sources, methodology and scope

    Credit spreads reflect market-implied risk and financing conditions rather than observed defaults or AI project returns. Quarterly leverage uses covered issuers with four consecutive EBITDA quarters. Rates, issuer mix, equity volatility and event risk may also move CDS; role comparisons do not establish causality. Higher covered issuance relative to US IG supply can indicate a larger absorption burden for credit investors. Compare this with leverage and CDS: stable leverage alongside heavy issuance is consistent with supply pressure, but does not establish its cause. Deteriorating leverage and wider spreads point to a different funding concern. Ratings, maturity, market liquidity and benchmark rolls also affect spreads. Sources, methodology and scope

  1. (1) Data source and reliability

    Bloomberg workbook issuer-month bond issuance amount and count through 2026-11, with matched US investment-grade corporate issuance through 2026-11. Both queries use USD amounts. The most recent month may be partial.

    S6

  2. (2) Methodology

    Sum covered issuer-month amounts into supply-chain sectors. Relative supply = covered issuance / US IG issuance × 100 on matched months. The period ratio divides sums, not average percentages. The numerator includes countries and ratings excluded from the benchmark, so this is not an exact market-share measure. Leave missing numerator months blank and exclude benchmark-only months from the ratio.

  3. (3) Scope and other necessary information

    Issuance measures access to funding, not issuer-specific AI use of proceeds or returns. Supply intensity alongside stable leverage can be consistent with absorption pressure, but issuance cannot identify the cause of CDS changes. A partial month cannot be compared directly with a full month. Bond issuance retains zero weight in the supplementary adjustment until coverage and normalization are resolved.

Sources and calculation boundaries

Company share = company TTM amount / sum of available company TTM amounts in the selected currency group. TTM sums four consecutive calendarized source quarters; missing quarters remain unavailable. March 2026 is the latest complete common TTM date for all 36 companies. June lacks complete observations for AMD, ASML and Lam Research.

EBITDA shares retain negative contributions; a nonpositive total has no percentage calculation. EBITDA is before depreciation, interest and taxes, and does not measure capital returns. Revenue totals include intercompany sales and must not be interpreted as AI market size or value added. Private lab annualized revenue estimates are excluded from this comparable listed-company calculation.

Reporting-currency groups: USD except ASML EUR, TSMC TWD, SK hynix/Samsung KRW and Tokyo Electron JPY. The current Currncy=USD parameter does not verify conversion. Global revenue/EBITDA shares are withheld.

Sources, methodology and scope

  1. (1) Data source and reliability

    Workbook daily stock returns and financial observations for 36 companies. Returns are compounded from December 31, 2025; no FX conversion. Missing daily values remain gaps. Credit coverage remains a smaller separate universe. Historical fundamental scores retain their original 32-company coverage and vintage.

    S1S4S5

  2. (2) Methodology

    Signal definitions: Market is the equal-weight selected-period return (Strong ≥10%, Constructive ≥3%, Mixed >−3%, otherwise Weak). Fundamental is the equal-weight composite from the Financial Resilience company screen (Strong ≥65, Resilient ≥50, Mixed ≥35, otherwise Fragile). CDS pressure averages 1M and 3M spread changes for covered issuers only (Rising ≥+3 bp, Easing ≤−3 bp); coverage is always shown. Stock returns are compounded from observed daily returns since December 31, 2025; missing observations are not zero-filled. Local listings use different trading calendars and retain individual observation dates. Structural links represent industry relationships rather than company-level supplier contracts or index weights.

  3. (3) Scope and other necessary information

    Industry connections do not establish supplier contracts or portfolio weights. Different coverage can affect comparisons. Prices, resilience and credit conditions are separate signals; none alone proves capital return.

METHODOLOGY & DATA DISCLOSURES

Signal construction and analytical scope.

The core index measures investment momentum. The supplementary overlay adds financial quality and credit conditions. The core includes frontier-lab annualized revenue levels in Monetization. Cash coverage and ROIC provide supplementary evidence on sustainability and returns.

Sources, methodology and scope

  1. (1) Data source and reliability

    S14
    Ramp AI Index — paid adoption and spending

    Saved data from Ramp’s public dashboard, retrieved 2026-11-23. Monthly observations through 2026-10. Paid adoption is the share of Ramp businesses with observed AI payments, not all U.S. businesses. Median spending is nominal USD per employee per month. Website JSON routes are undocumented; the supported API requires credentials. Provider adoption can overlap. Token volumes come from the separate Ramp TSM sample, aggregated from published model series. Daily rolling-seven-day fields cover a narrower provider sample and are not treated as daily observations. Spend-share and sector/provider breakdowns remain context. Spending calibration has 20 observations through June 2026. The publisher’s weekly token series runs through 2026-11-15. The matched index retains the archived Sunday-ending series through 2026-11-15.

    S1
    Indexlist.xlsx — Index Price Value

    Completed workbook inputs through 2026-09. DRAM and NAND exports, TSMC revenue, equipment orders, imports, construction and high-tech activity feed Infrastructure. The constituent rows show each series’ latest scored input date.

    S2
    Consolidated U.S. hyperscaler CapEx workbook

    The last approved combined CapEx score uses the calendar quarter ending 2026-06-30. The five-company scenario uses accounting-basis adjustments to project the score. The heatmaps mark these projections with E.

    S3
    China cloud CapEx source collection

    Tencent operating CapEx, Alibaba quarterly CapEx and Baidu cash CapEx through 2026Q2. RMB is primary; approximate values, inferred AI shares and issuer-specific definitions remain labeled.

    S4
    Indexlist.xlsx — AI 5yrCDS Value

    Bloomberg-implied issuer 5Y CDS through 2026-11-24 and the IBOXUMAE Curncy benchmark through 2026-11-24, with latest issuer ratings dated 2026-09-30. The daily analysis compares spreads only where the benchmark is available; the supplementary credit adjustment and value-chain signals retain their labeled 16 Sep vintage.

    S5
    Indexlist.xlsx — Supply Chain Financial Value

    Latest reported financial metrics for 36 issuers, including TSMC, SK hynix, Samsung Electronics and Tokyo Electron. Stock observations use Supply Chain Stock Value daily returns and USD market caps through 2026-11-24. Market sector returns use lagged daily cap weights; the treemap uses latest caps. Three missing opening caps use first available proxies; their partial opening return histories are disclosed. Missing interim reports are labeled and receive no freshness penalty.

    S6
    Indexlist.xlsx — Bond Issuance Value

    Saved issuer-month amounts and issue counts through 2026-11, with matched US IG corporate issuance through 2026-11. Both queries use USD amounts. Covered issuers include other countries and ratings, so the displayed ratio measures relative issuance scale rather than a strict US IG market share. Missing issuer-month records are shown as gaps. The most recent month may be partial.

    S11
    Epoch AI — AI chip owners, users and data centers

    Owner-level chip estimates through 2026Q1, year-end 2025 lab-use estimates and 96 facility records as of 2026-11-06. H100e, power and workload values are modeled estimates rather than measures of realized utilization or financial return.

    S9
    OpenRouter daily rankings

    Source: OpenRouter (openrouter.ai/rankings), saved as of 2026-11-23. The daily API history runs from January 2025 through 2026-11-22, with model-level top-50 rows and an aggregate long-tail bucket. Adoption scores growth in routed volume across complete matched windows. Monetization uses estimated spending growth based on catalog rates and a daily blended rate for unresolved traffic. The dashboard retains source coverage dates for both signals. OpenRouter covers traffic routed through its platform. Dataset methodology

    S10
    Epoch AI and sourced disclosures — OpenAI and Anthropic

    Latest saved run-rate disclosure dated 2026-10-08. The core scores each lab’s log annualized revenue level using its own disclosure history. The research charts distinguish ARR, run rates and recognized quarterly revenue.

    S12
    Epoch AI — frontier models and machine-learning hardware

    Frontier-model training-cost estimates in constant 2023 dollars and selected accelerator specifications. Models without cost estimates are excluded. Dataset documentation

    S13
    Task observations and Epoch AI — cost per successful task

    Model-version prices are combined with benchmark success rates and assumed tokens per attempt. Protocol and model-class differences limit direct comparison.

  2. (2) Methodology

    01

    Prepare the scoring signals

    Adoption rates use percentage levels. Token usage compares each source’s trailing three-month average with the previous month’s three-month average. Other signals use their specified spending, growth, price or revenue-level measure.

    02

    Normalize to 0–100

    OpenRouter and Ramp token growth use source-specific percentile ranks. Other signals use 50 + 15 × z-score, bounded to 0–100. A score of 50 is the baseline median for token growth and the baseline mean for the other signals. Monthly calibration uses saved history through 2026-06.

    03

    Combine four pillars

    Each pillar has 25% nominal core weight. Adoption splits its weight equally between breadth and usage. Monetization allocates 60% of its pillar weight to business paid demand, 20% to consumer card spending growth and 20% to lab revenue scale. Hyperscalers scores combined CapEx growth. Infrastructure scores physical activity and hardware pricing. Available constituents absorb missing weight within each pillar. Available pillars share the core weight equally.

    04

    Apply the supplementary adjustment

    The adjusted score adds bounded fundamental and credit deltas to the core when both coverage thresholds are met. Bond issuance carries zero weight in the adjustment.

    SUPPLEMENTARY ADJUSTMENT FORMULA

    Adjusted = clamp(Core + Fundamental Δ + Credit Δ, 0, 100)

    Fundamental Δ = 10% × (median Fundamental Composite − 50)

    Credit score = clamp(50 + 2.5 × CDS Change Signal, 0, 100)

    Credit Δ = 10% × (Credit score − 50)

    Each satellite delta is bounded to ±5 points. The supplementary adjustment uses fixed multipliers. The adjusted score is withheld below financial/CDS coverage thresholds.

  3. (3) Scope and other necessary information

    Limits that matter for interpretation

    • Preserve Bloomberg units, seasonal-adjustment flags, release dates and point-in-time vintages.
    • Replace PREV-filled observations with explicit freshness and stale-value controls.
    • Backfill January 2026 bond issuance before publishing rolling-12-month YoY.
    • Add sector-neutral and size-neutral tests to the financial screen; cap extreme CapEx ranks only after sensitivity analysis.
    • Run alternative pillar weights, outlier controls and benchmark-relative backtests before integrating satellites.
    • Separate actual and forecast atmosphere indices before adding forward quarters.
    • A global aggregate requires consistent FX conversion, CapEx definitions, constituent weights and missing-proxy rules.
